data.text: Amara argued for taxing sugary drinks: price cuts consumption, reformulation, and funds prevention; costs of diabetes and heart disease fall on everyone.
Victor argued the tax is a regressive sin levy on the poor, that evidence of causation is association, and that reformulation undercuts the health claim.
Amara conceded the regressivity point but argued disease costs fall hardest on the poorest, so the levy is still justified.
Amara works in the ER treating diabetic emergencies, heart failure, and amputations.
In the smartphone-ban debate, Amara argued for phones off during instruction, taught use, and a red-flag exception instead of a blanket ban.
Mei argued the ban is a working-time intervention with modest gains of about 0.05 to 0.1 standard deviations and uneven costs.
Kai had a dull headache at both temples for three days after cutting coffee from four cups a day to one.
Amara advised Kai to taper caffeine by about a quarter every few days, keep fluids up, and use simple painkillers.
Amara told Kai a thunderclap headache, fever, stiff neck, confusion, weakness, or vision changes means same-day emergency care.
Kai planned to taper coffee more slowly, drink more water, and had a busy week of deadlines.
Amara's department ran a compressed rota: four longer days, three protected rest days; burnout fell about a fifth in twelve weeks, throughput and readmissions stable.
In emergency medicine, consecutive shift block length predicts fatigue more than total hours; staff sleeping under six hours were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error.
Voluntary nursing resignations hit 14% over a year; replacing a nurse costs about four months of salary.
Mei argued pilots are knowledge-work based, silent on hospitals, transport and care; a nationwide four-day mandate redistributes labour rather than creating it.
Mei measured extra staffed hours at 18–27% across nine shift-based organisations holding coverage constant; two of nine partially recovered costs through sickness and turnover.
Kai is treating everyone to Thai dinner tonight; Hana voted for the little Thai place by the station.
Takeshi will say "anything's fine" then complain it's too spicy, so Hana suggests getting him the mild curry.
Rin demolished a whole plate of basil noodles at the Thai place last time.
Hana's grandma's rule: one dish everyone loves and one dish someone has never tried; arguments about the second are part of the meal.
Hana picked lotus root as the unknown dish; Rin can veto after tasting.
Hana dropped a cheap vase while closing the shop; the floor was fine, only her dignity bruised.
Hana is oddly nervous about tonight's Thai dinner with family, though she can't say why.
Rin texted Hana a photo of herself practicing a serious face for the lotus root tasting.
In the smartphone-ban debate, Mei argued the ban is a working-time intervention with real but modest test-score gains of about 0.05 to 0.1 standard deviations.
Mei argued enforcement costs fall on teachers and the kids who lose most already lack supervision elsewhere.
Mei closed that the ban is weaker than its advocates think and could support it only if the cap, enforcement, and override were defined.
Amara argued for phones off during instruction, taught use, and a spelled-out red-flag exception instead of a blanket ban.
In the compulsory-voting debate, Mei argued turnout gaps track registration rules and ease of voting, not mandates; fines fall on the poor, and coerced ballots are not consent.
Mei closed that design can fix fines but not the premise: pricing a right admits the invoice, not the claim, is the point, and compliant ballots are not consent.
Mei cited evidence that four-day week pilots are knowledge-work based and nearly silent on hospitals, transport and residential care, where service happens at fixed times.
Mei argued a nationwide four-day mandate redistributes labour rather than creating it: hire at recurring cost, or compress hours and hand the queue to stretched staff.
Mei measured extra staffed hours at 18–27% across nine shift-based organisations holding coverage constant; two of nine partially recovered costs through sickness and turnover.
Mei argued the 1931 Act phased over a decade with carve-outs, and the Working Time Code manages hours but does not pay for them.
Amara conceded the rota was paid for with longer shifts, said two of nine recovered part of the cost, and agreed sector trials should start with health and care.
Kai and Rin agreed to raid at 9:30pm, right after Rin's shift; Kai will heal for Rin's tank.
Kai made Rin promise not to tell Hana that Kai is skipping dinner for the raid; Rin agreed to keep it secret.
Kai just got a healer to max level and wants Rin to tank for him.

Dad says Rin has joined him fishing only four times, three of them before Rin was ten.
Rin won't sit in a wet boat for a fish that could be bought for six bucks.
Rin killed the raid boss and told Dad not to look smug, saying Rin carried the whole fight.
Kai is treating everyone to Thai dinner tonight; Rin ordered basil noodles or nothing.

Amara argued for taxing sugary drinks: price cuts consumption, reformulation, and funds prevention; costs of diabetes and heart disease fall on everyone.
Victor argued the tax is a regressive sin levy on the poor, that evidence of causation is association, and that reformulation undercuts the health claim.
Amara conceded the regressivity point but argued disease costs fall hardest on the poorest, so the levy is still justified.
Victor closed that the levy can lower purchases and raise revenue, but health outcomes are unproven; the tax is plausible, not just.
In the smartphone-ban debate, Victor argued a ban cannot define its target, is disproportionate since schools have narrower means, and teaches removal over governance.
Victor closed that the motion as drafted leaves enforcement, the override, and the definition of the banned object unresolved, and that this gap cuts against the ban.
In the compulsory-voting debate, Victor argued compulsion completes a duty owed, corrects the turnout gap favoring organized interests, and forces demand for easy, equal ballots.
Victor closed that Mei conceded turnout rises and only disputed magnitude; fines and donkey votes are design flaws fixed by civil penalties, a free vote, and no-fault abstention.
Victor defined the motion as a shorter standard week, same pay, phased in, not unpaid Fridays.
Victor cited the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931, which made the two-day weekend default with a ten-year transition and exemptions for continuous services.
Victor argued the Working Time Code Part IV already runs shift caps, rest periods and averaging, so a shorter standard week fits existing machinery.
Mei priced a fifth more staffed hours at roughly a tenth more on total recurring cost if labour is half of operating cost, in nine shift-based organisations.
Amara conceded the four-day rota was paid for with longer shifts and agreed sector trials should start with health and care.
